triage.reason: Acute myocardial infarction with classic chest pain, ECG changes and troponin elevation; core emergency case with a critical differential.

demographics: Men have a higher risk at younger ages; women's risk rises after menopause and their first event is often later in life
Black adults have higher rates of heart attack and death from heart attack than White adults
South Asian adults have higher rates of premature coronary disease
Risk is higher in people with lower income and less access to preventive care

risk_factors.text: Coronary artery disease or prior heart attack
Cigarette smoking or long-term secondhand smoke exposure
Age (men 45 and older, women 55 and older)
Family history of early heart attack in a first-degree relative
Obesity, especially with a large waist
Chronic inflammatory conditions such as rheumatoid arthritis or lupus

family_history: Heart attack or sudden cardiac death in a father or brother before age 55
Heart attack or sudden cardiac death in a mother or sister before age 65
High cholesterol that runs in the family
social_history: Cocaine, methamphetamine or other stimulant use
Low income or limited access to medical care

chief_complaints.text: I have pressure in my chest
My chest feels heavy and tight
My chest is burning like heartburn
My left arm and jaw are aching

hpi.onset: Sudden, often at rest or with mild activity; many wake up with it
hpi.duration: Usually more than 20 minutes and often an hour or more by the time help is called
hpi.progression: Builds over minutes to a steady, severe discomfort that does not fully go away; may come in waves but never resolves completely
hpi.location: Center of the chest, behind the breastbone; may be felt on the left side or in the upper abdomen
hpi.radiation: To the left arm or both arms, neck, jaw, shoulder, back or upper abdomen
hpi.quality: Pressure, squeezing, tightness, heaviness or a band-like constriction; sometimes burning or indigestion-like
hpi.severity: Moderate to severe, often 7–10/10; some describe it as the worst discomfort they have felt
hpi.timing: Constant, not sharp or fleeting; does not change with position or breathing
relieving: Nitroglycerin, though often only partially and briefly

associated_symptoms.text: Feeling of doom or that something is very wrong

pertinent_negatives: Sharp pain that gets worse with a deep breath or when lying flat
Pain reproduced by pressing on the chest wall
Pain that changes with twisting or bending the torso
Burning pain that rises from the stomach after meals and is relieved by antacids
Tearing pain that moves from the chest to the back between the shoulder blades
Sudden one-sided pleuritic pain with leg swelling
Recent heavy lifting or vomiting followed by severe chest pain

argues_against: Infection such as pneumonia or pericarditis

negatives: Chest pain reproduced by pressing on the chest
argues_against: Deep vein thrombosis with pulmonary embolism
Aortic dissection involving the carotid arteries

negatives: Symptoms only when thinking about stress

atypical.how_it_differs: May have little or no chest pain and instead present with sudden shortness of breath, weakness, confusion, fainting or a fall.
missing_classic_features: Radiation to the arm or jaw

atypical.how_it_differs: Nerve damage from diabetes can blunt the pain, so the first sign may be shortness of breath, nausea, sweating or a very high blood sugar.
Rare, but when it happens it is often caused by coronary artery dissection or spasm rather than a plaque rupture; symptoms may be blamed on normal late-pregnancy discomfort.
Chest discomfort may be vague and attributed to reflux or muscle strain, and shortness of breath on exertion may be dismissed as being out of shape.

general.mild: Anxious, pale, mildly diaphoretic but able to speak in full sentences
general.moderate: Distressed, diaphoretic, clutching the chest, speaking in short phrases
general.severe: Ill-appearing, cold and clammy, pale or gray, restless, speaking in words
general.critical: Toxic-appearing, mottled, obtunded or agitated, in extremis

findings.maneuver: Inspect and touch the skin of the forehead, palms and trunk
findings.finding: Cold, clammy, diaphoretic skin

findings.maneuver: Inspect the conjunctivae, palms and mucous membranes
findings.finding: Pale, ashen or gray skin color

findings.maneuver: Auscultate the apex with the bell while the patient lies in the left lateral position
findings.finding: Third heart sound (S3 gallop)

findings.maneuver: Auscultate all valve areas and listen for a new murmur
findings.finding: New systolic murmur, suggesting mitral regurgitation from papillary muscle dysfunction or a ventricular septal defect

findings.maneuver: Auscultate the apex with the bell
findings.finding: Fourth heart sound (S4 gallop)

findings.maneuver: Inspect the internal jugular vein at 45 degrees with the head turned slightly away
findings.finding: Elevated jugular venous pressure
Bibasilar crackles from pulmonary congestion

findings.maneuver: Press the dorsum of each foot and the pretibial area for 5 seconds
findings.finding: Pitting edema of the lower extremities

findings.maneuver: Palpate the anterior chest wall and reproduce any area of reported pain
findings.finding: No reproducible chest wall tenderness

findings.maneuver: Ask the patient to lean forward, lie flat, and take a deep breath
findings.finding: No change in the chest discomfort with position or respiration

findings.maneuver: Ask the patient to take a deep breath and cough
findings.finding: No sharp pleuritic pain and no focal chest pain with inspiration

findings.maneuver: Inspect and palpate both calves for asymmetry, swelling and tenderness
findings.finding: No unilateral calf swelling or tenderness

findings.maneuver: Measure the temperature and inspect for signs of infection
findings.finding: No fever and no focal infectious signs

findings.maneuver: Ask about the character and migration of the pain and palpate peripheral pulses symmetrically
findings.finding: No tearing pain radiating to the back and no pulse deficit between arms

labs.caveat: The key test. A rise and fall over serial draws is what defines myocardial injury; a single mildly elevated value can also come from kidney disease, heart failure or sepsis. Values are higher in larger infarcts and peak around 12–24 hours.
Nonspecific; troponin is preferred. Useful mainly to gauge infarct size or to suggest reinfarction when troponin is already elevated.
Elevated when the infarct causes heart failure or significant ventricular dysfunction; helps risk-stratify but does not diagnose the infarct.
A stress leukocytosis is common in the first days and does not mean infection.
Stress hyperglycemia is common and worsens outcome; also screens for undiagnosed diabetes.
Baseline kidney function is needed before contrast for angiography; a rise can also reflect cardiogenic shock or contrast nephropathy.
Low potassium from vomiting, diuretics or catecholamine shift predisposes to arrhythmia and must be corrected.
Guides high-intensity statin dosing; may be drawn early or within 24 hours of admission.
Identifies unrecognized diabetes or prediabetes that needs treatment after discharge.
Anemia worsens ischemia and may be from bleeding, especially if the patient is on anticoagulants or antiplatelets.
Needed before thrombolysis or invasive procedures and to assess bleeding risk.
Prolonged with heparin or a coagulopathy; relevant before procedures.
Often elevated in myocardial infarction but is not diagnostic; order only when pulmonary embolism or aortic dissection is being considered.

findings.finding: ST-segment elevation in a territorial pattern (contiguous leads), the hallmark of an acute STEMI
ST-segment depression, the typical finding in NSTEMI and unstable angina
Hyperacute peaked T waves, an early sign before ST elevation appears
T-wave inversion in the affected territory
Reciprocal ST depression in leads opposite the infarct (supports true STEMI over pericarditis)
Pathologic Q waves in the affected territory, indicating completed infarction
New left bundle branch block or new bifascicular block, which can mask ST changes and is treated like a STEMI when symptoms fit
Second- or third-degree atrioventricular block, especially with inferior infarction
Sinus tachycardia from pain, anxiety or heart failure
Ventricular tachycardia or ventricular fibrillation, a cause of sudden death
Atrial fibrillation, often transient
Prolonged QT interval, which raises the risk of torsades de pointes
Normal or nondiagnostic ECG, which does not exclude myocardial infarction and requires serial tracings and troponin

imaging.preferred_when: All patients with suspected or confirmed myocardial infarction, at the bedside in the emergency department or within 24 hours

findings.text: Regional wall motion abnormality in the territory of the infarct-related artery
Left ventricular thrombus, especially with anterior infarction
Mitral regurgitation from papillary muscle dysfunction
Ventricular septal defect or free wall rupture with pericardial tamponade

imaging.preferred_when: STEMI for immediate reperfusion; NSTEMI or unstable angina with high-risk features

findings.text: Acute occlusion or severe stenosis of a coronary artery with thrombus
Culprit lesion identified and treated with percutaneous coronary intervention

imaging.preferred_when: Low-risk chest pain when acute coronary syndrome is possible but troponin and ECG are not diagnostic

findings.text: Coronary artery calcification and atherosclerotic plaque
No significant coronary stenosis, making acute coronary syndrome unlikely
Usually normal heart size and clear lungs
Pulmonary venous congestion or edema when there is heart failure

imaging.preferred_when: Suspected aortic dissection (tearing pain, pulse deficit, widened mediastinum)

findings.text: Intimal flap dividing the aortic lumen

imaging.preferred_when: Suspected pulmonary embolism (pleuritic pain, hypoxemia, leg swelling)

findings.text: Filling defect in a pulmonary artery

initial.why: The key blood test; a rise and fall confirms myocardial injury. Draw serially.
Looks for anemia and stress leukocytosis and gives a platelet count before antiplatelet therapy
Baseline kidney function, potassium and glucose before contrast and medications
Baseline clotting studies before anticoagulation or procedures
Screens for diabetes that needs treatment
Shows regional wall motion abnormality and ejection fraction at the bedside
Looks for heart failure, widened mediastinum and other causes of chest pain
initial.only_if: alternative diagnoses such as aortic dissection, pneumonia or heart failure are being considered

confirmatory.why: Defines the culprit lesion and allows immediate percutaneous coronary intervention in STEMI and high-risk NSTEMI

supporting.only_if: dyspnea, crackles or suspected heart failure

supporting.why: Estimates infarct size or suggests reinfarction
supporting.only_if: troponin is already elevated and reinfarction is suspected
pleuritic pain, hypoxemia or leg swelling suggests pulmonary embolism

supporting.why: Evaluates low-risk chest pain when troponin and ECG are nondiagnostic
supporting.only_if: acute coronary syndrome is possible but troponin and ECG are not diagnostic
tearing pain, pulse deficit or widened mediastinum suggests dissection

not_indicated.why: No role in chest pain unless a urinary cause is suspected
Not needed unless the pain is epigastric and pancreatitis is suspected

decision_points: Obtain and interpret a 12-lead ECG within 10 minutes of arrival; repeat every 15–30 minutes if nondiagnostic
ST elevation on ECG with symptoms is a STEMI and goes to immediate reperfusion without waiting for troponin
Serial troponin at 0 and 1–3 hours; a rise and fall is required to confirm myocardial infarction
Check for contraindications to thrombolysis and anticoagulation before giving them
Bedside echocardiogram early to assess ejection fraction and mechanical complications
Pregnancy test before radiation-based imaging in anyone who could be pregnant

criteria.name: Fourth Universal Definition of Myocardial Infarction
criteria.summary: Myocardial infarction is diagnosed when there is a rise and fall of cardiac troponin with at least one value above the 99th percentile, together with evidence of myocardial ischemia: symptoms, new ECG changes, new Q waves, or imaging showing new loss of viable myocardium or a new regional wall motion abnormality. It is classified by cause, including plaque rupture (type 1) and supply-demand mismatch (type 2).
items: Rise and fall of troponin above the 99th percentile
Imaging evidence of new regional wall motion abnormality or loss of viable myocardium

differential.name: Unstable angina
differential.why_considered: Same atherosclerotic cause and same symptom pattern, but no myocardial necrosis
differential.trigger: Chest pressure at rest or with minimal exertion that is new or worsening, with a normal or nondiagnostic troponin

history: Chest discomfort that is new, more frequent, longer or now occurs at rest
Discomfort relieved by rest or nitroglycerin
No prolonged unrelieved episode
labs: No rise and fall of troponin
ecg: Transient ST depression or T-wave inversion during pain
ECG may be normal between episodes

differential.name: Aortic dissection
differential.why_considered: Severe chest pain that can radiate to the back and mimic myocardial infarction
differential.trigger: Sudden tearing or ripping pain that moves from the chest to the back between the shoulder blades, with a pulse or blood pressure difference between arms

history: Abrupt onset of severe tearing or ripping pain
Pain migrates from the chest to the back or abdomen
History of hypertension, connective tissue disease or cocaine use
exam: Pulse deficit or blood pressure difference between arms
Focal neurologic deficit if the carotid arteries are involved
labs: Troponin usually normal unless the dissection involves a coronary ostium
imaging: Intimal flap on CT angiography of the aorta

differential.name: Pulmonary embolism
differential.why_considered: Sudden shortness of breath and chest pain with risk factors for venous thromboembolism
differential.trigger: Pleuritic chest pain with hypoxemia, tachycardia and a swollen tender calf

history: Sudden dyspnea and pleuritic pain
Recent surgery, immobility, cancer or prior venous thromboembolism
Calf pain or swelling
labs: Troponin usually normal or only mildly elevated
imaging: Filling defect in a pulmonary artery on CT pulmonary angiography
ecg: S1Q3T3 pattern or right axis deviation

differential.name: Pericarditis
differential.why_considered: Chest pain with ECG changes that can be mistaken for myocardial infarction

history: Sharp pain worse with deep breathing and when lying flat
Pain improved by sitting up and leaning forward
Recent viral illness
exam: Pain reproduced by pressure over the sternum or precordium
labs: Troponin usually normal or only mildly elevated
Markers of inflammation such as CRP or ESR may be elevated
ecg: Diffuse concave ST elevation without a territorial pattern

differential.name: Gastroesophageal reflux disease
differential.why_considered: Burning chest discomfort that can feel like a heart attack

history: Burning pain after meals or when lying down
Relief with antacids
No exertional pattern
exam: No diaphoresis or signs of heart failure

differential.name: Esophageal spasm
differential.why_considered: Severe squeezing chest pain that can be indistinguishable from cardiac ischemia

history: Pain often occurs with swallowing or at rest
May be relieved by nitroglycerin, which can be misleading
No exertional pattern
exam: Normal cardiac and chest wall exam

differential.name: Costochondritis
differential.why_considered: Chest wall pain that can be mistaken for cardiac pain

history: Sharp, localized pain worse with movement, coughing or deep breathing
Pain reproduced by pressing on the chest wall
No radiation to the arm or jaw
exam: Reproducible tenderness over the costochondral junctions
No diaphoresis or signs of heart failure

differential.name: Pneumothorax
differential.why_considered: Sudden chest pain and shortness of breath

history: Sudden sharp one-sided pain
Pain worse with breathing
Recent trauma or known lung disease
exam: Decreased breath sounds and hyperresonance on the affected side
imaging: Visible pleural line and absent lung markings on chest x-ray
No pneumothorax on CT if uncertain

severity.mild: Small infarct, no heart failure, hemodynamically stable, no arrhythmia; troponin mildly elevated, ECG shows ST depression or T-wave inversion
severity.moderate: Larger infarct with mild heart failure or ongoing pain; troponin moderately elevated, ECG shows ST elevation or significant ST depression, may need urgent reperfusion
severity.severe: Large infarct with pulmonary edema, hypotension or significant arrhythmia; troponin markedly elevated, ECG shows extensive ST elevation or new bundle branch block
severity.critical: Cardiogenic shock, ventricular fibrillation or mechanical complication such as papillary muscle rupture, ventricular septal defect or free wall rupture; troponin very high, patient in extremis

red_flags.meaning: Acute STEMI; needs immediate reperfusion therapy
Large infarct or mechanical complication; needs urgent intervention
Life-threatening arrhythmia; needs immediate defibrillation and advanced cardiac life support

red_flags.finding: New murmur or acute pulmonary edema
red_flags.meaning: Mechanical complication such as papillary muscle rupture or ventricular septal defect

red_flags.finding: Sudden severe tearing pain radiating to the back

complications.name: Arrhythmias
clues: ECG shows ventricular tachycardia, ventricular fibrillation or heart block

complications.name: Ventricular septal defect
clues: Thrill at the left sternal border

complications.name: Free wall rupture
clues: Pericardial effusion with tamponade on echocardiogram

special_populations.differences: May present without chest pain, with sudden shortness of breath, weakness, confusion, fainting or a fall; higher mortality and more atypical symptoms.
Neuropathy can blunt pain, so the first sign may be dyspnea, nausea, sweating or hyperglycemia; higher risk of silent infarction.

Rare, but when it occurs it is often caused by coronary artery dissection or spasm rather than plaque rupture; symptoms may be attributed to normal pregnancy discomfort; radiation-based imaging should be avoided when possible.
Higher risk of contrast nephropathy; need careful hydration and consideration of alternative imaging or treatment strategies.
Chest discomfort may be vague and attributed to reflux or muscle strain; shortness of breath on exertion may be dismissed as being out of shape.

key_questions.question: What does the discomfort feel like, and where is it?
key_questions.looking_for: Pressure, squeezing, tightness or heaviness in the center of the chest behind the breastbone

key_questions.question: When did it start, and is it still there now?
key_questions.looking_for: Sudden onset more than 20 minutes ago and still present; ongoing pain means ongoing ischemia

key_questions.question: Does it spread anywhere?
key_questions.looking_for: Radiation to the left or both arms, neck, jaw, shoulder, back or upper abdomen

key_questions.question: Did it come on at rest or with exertion?
key_questions.looking_for: Often at rest or with mild activity; many wake up with it

key_questions.question: Does anything make it better or worse, like rest, nitroglycerin, position or breathing?
key_questions.looking_for: Rest and nitroglycerin help only partially or briefly; no change with position or breathing

key_questions.question: Are you short of breath, sweaty, nauseated or lightheaded?
key_questions.looking_for: Shortness of breath, cold clammy sweat, nausea or vomiting, dizziness

key_questions.question: Have you ever had chest pain, a heart attack, angina, a stent or bypass surgery?
key_questions.looking_for: Known coronary artery disease or prior myocardial infarction raises the probability sharply

key_questions.question: Do you have high blood pressure, high cholesterol, diabetes or kidney disease?
key_questions.looking_for: Major modifiable risk factors that support the diagnosis

key_questions.question: Do you smoke, or have you smoked?
key_questions.looking_for: Current or past smoking, a strong risk factor

key_questions.question: Has anyone in your family had a heart attack or sudden cardiac death, and at what age?
key_questions.looking_for: Father or brother before 55, mother or sister before 65

key_questions.question: Do you use cocaine, methamphetamine or other stimulants?
key_questions.looking_for: Stimulant use, which can cause coronary spasm or thrombosis

key_questions.question: Is the pain sharp and worse when you take a deep breath or lie flat, or does pressing on your chest reproduce it?
key_questions.looking_for: Absent; these features point away from myocardial infarction toward pericarditis or chest wall pain

key_questions.question: Did the pain start suddenly and tear or rip through to your back?
key_questions.looking_for: Absent; tearing pain radiating to the back suggests aortic dissection, a must-not-miss look-alike

reasoning_points: Chest pressure lasting more than 20 minutes, often at rest, with radiation to the arm, neck or jaw
Associated shortness of breath, cold diaphoresis, nausea or a sense of doom
Cardiac risk factors such as age, smoking, hypertension, diabetes, hyperlipidemia, prior coronary disease or early family history
ECG showing territorial ST elevation, ST depression or T-wave inversion, with reciprocal changes supporting infarction
Rise and fall of serial high-sensitivity troponin above the 99th percentile confirming myocardial injury
Echocardiogram showing a new regional wall motion abnormality in the territory of the infarct-related artery
Alternative life-threatening causes excluded: aortic dissection, pulmonary embolism and pericarditis
Recognition that ST elevation with symptoms is a STEMI needing immediate reperfusion without waiting for troponin

easy: Older man with classic pressure-like chest pain radiating to the left arm
Cold diaphoresis and nausea with the pain
Known coronary artery disease or prior myocardial infarction
ECG shows clear territorial ST elevation with reciprocal depression
Troponin markedly elevated on the first draw
medium: NSTEMI with ST depression or T-wave inversion rather than ST elevation
Diabetic patient with blunted pain presenting with dyspnea, nausea and sweating
Pain described as heartburn or indigestion rather than pressure
Normal or nondiagnostic initial ECG requiring serial tracings and repeat troponin
Woman or older adult with fatigue and shortness of breath as the main complaint
hard: Older adult presenting with confusion, weakness or a fall and no chest pain
New left bundle branch block masking the ST changes
Inferior infarct with vagal symptoms, bradycardia and hypotension
Cocaine-associated coronary spasm or thrombosis in a younger patient
Chest pain with a competing diagnosis such as aortic dissection, pulmonary embolism or pericarditis
Troponin elevated from another cause such as kidney disease, heart failure or sepsis, requiring careful interpretation
